mc.prompt: Which chain best explains one way an STI can reduce fertility?
mc.answer: Infection → inflammation and scarring → disrupted transport
options: Infection → conversion of LH into sperm → duct blockage
Infection → immediate menstruation in every case → fertilization
Infection → inflammation and scarring → disrupted transport
Infection → guaranteed loss of all gametes → higher fertility
mc.cue: Look for a mechanism linking tissue damage with normal reproductive function.
mc.explanation: Inflammation and scarring can damage reproductive passages and interfere with transport.

mc.answer: Hormonal contraception and STI risk reduction are different functions
options: All contraceptive methods prevent every STI
Hormonal contraception and STI risk reduction are different functions
mc.cue: Separate pathogens, hormone signals and physical barriers.
mc.explanation: A method that prevents ovulation does not necessarily reduce exposure to infectious organisms.

writing.prompt: Explain how an STI could interfere with reproduction while gamete and hormone production continue.
writing.model: Infection may cause inflammation and scarring in a duct such as an oviduct or epididymis. Damage can interfere with maturation or transport even when gonads continue producing cells or hormones.
criteria: Explains tissue damage and its functional effect.

writing.prompt: A student says, “If a method prevents pregnancy, it must prevent STIs too.” Explain the flaw using two different mechanisms.
writing.model: Hormonal contraception can prevent an LH surge and ovulation; it does not form a pathogen barrier. Condoms reduce contact with some infectious material and also obstruct sperm passage, but do not eliminate every infection risk. Conception and transmission are different processes.
criteria: Contrasts hormonal action with barrier action without promising complete protection.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Normal ovulation, damaged oviduct
worked.scenario: A hypothetical case describes normal ovulation and a scarred, blocked oviduct after an infection.
steps: Identify what still occurs: the ovary releases an oocyte.
Locate the problem: transport through the oviduct is impaired.
Explain the consequence: sperm and the oocyte may not meet, or movement toward the uterus may be disrupted.
Do not overstate: this description does not show that FSH, LH or ovarian hormone production has stopped. The immediate explanation is tissue damage along the pathway.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Apply the explanation
guided.instruction: Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

items.prompt: Why might the absence of symptoms fail to rule out an STI?
options: Only hormone-producing cells can be infected
items.hint: Consider whether every infection produces visible signs.
items.explanation: Some infections produce no obvious symptoms, so symptoms alone cannot establish infection status.

items.prompt: Which consequence most directly follows scarring that blocks an oviduct?
options: Automatic loss of all ovarian chromosomes
Direct conversion of bacteria into hormones
items.hint: Use the normal function of an oviduct.
items.explanation: Scarring can obstruct the pathway where gametes meet and early development moves toward the uterus.

new_optional_model: A has a signalling/ovulation problem: no oocyte is released in the stated cycle. B has a transport problem despite release of an oocyte. Removing an infection does not by itself restore the LH surge in A or reverse established scarring in B. The models need evidence about the affected process, not an assumption that one intervention fixes every cause of reduced fertility.
